CT420 Revision

Soft Real-time and Multimedia

Judge perceived quality by delay variation, loss and adaptation rather than a single bandwidth number.

Rapid exam refresher

  • Latency/jitter/loss/throughput influence QoS.
  • intrinsic vs perceived.
  • jitter buffer trades delay/smoothness.
  • decompose budget.

Purpose, scope and examiner demand

Multimedia often tolerates an occasional miss but users notice stalls, late audio and unstable interaction. A good answer connects network behaviour to user experience and the mitigation's cost.

Exam focus by part

  • Latency/jitter/loss/throughput influence QoS.
  • intrinsic vs perceived.
  • jitter buffer trades delay/smoothness.
  • decompose budget.

Question-demand diagnosis and answer plan

  1. Classify the flow: interactive audio, video streaming, cloud gaming, or bulk transfer.
  2. Separate latency, jitter, loss, bitrate and throughput.
  3. Say which QoS notion is affected: intrinsic technical quality or perceived user quality.
  4. Choose a mitigation and explain its trade-off.

Question-type cues

  • Application cue: Compare fixed/adaptive VoIP jitter buffers.
  • Analysis cue: Cloud gaming feels slow variably.

Definitions, notation and discriminating comparisons

  • Jitter buffer: stores arriving media briefly to smooth delay variation; more buffering reduces glitches but adds latency.
  • QoS: measurable delivery quality; QoE: user-perceived quality.
  • Codec: compresses media; adaptive bitrate changes quality to match conditions.
  • End-to-end delay is capture + encode + queue + transmit + decode + playout. The budget, not just one component, matters.

Step-by-step methods and solution routes

For a voice call, suppose network delay varies between 30 and 70 ms. A 40 ms jitter buffer can smooth this variation, so playout is steadier. But it adds playout delay, so an interactive call may feel less responsive. If loss is the main issue, retransmission may arrive too late; concealment or a lower bitrate can be more appropriate.

Reasoning checkpoints

  1. Use and justify: Latency/jitter/loss/throughput influence QoS.
  2. Use and justify: intrinsic vs perceived.
  3. Use and justify: jitter buffer trades delay/smoothness.
  4. Use and justify: decompose budget.

Worked examples and method extensions

Question

A cloud game has good average bandwidth but feels laggy and jerky. Give two likely causes and controls.

Model answer

Variable queueing can create jitter and a high end-to-end latency, even with good average bandwidth. Use queue management/priority treatment and reduce the encode or playout buffer where safe. Packet loss can cause visible frame gaps; adaptive bitrate, forward error correction or concealment may help. The answer should note that buffering trades smoothness for interaction delay.

Exam-paper-led practice

Practice question 1 [medium/hard]

Scenario and demand: A VoIP path varies from 30–70 ms network delay. Compare a fixed 40 ms jitter buffer with an adaptive buffer. [8 marks]

Question-demand diagnosis and fastest route: A fixed 40 ms buffer can smooth the observed variation if correctly sized, giving steady playout but adding interaction delay even when the network is good. An adaptive buffer changes target delay as jitter changes, reducing underflows or unnecessary latency but needs stable estimation and bounded adjustment. Packet loss may need concealment/FEC, not ever more buffering. Trap: a jitter buffer does not increase bandwidth or repair arbitrary loss.

Practice question 2 [medium/hard]

Scenario and demand: Cloud gaming has high average bandwidth but feels slow and jerky. Diagnose QoS versus QoE and choose controls. [9 marks]

Question-demand diagnosis and fastest route: Decompose input, encode, queue, network, decode and playout delay; variable queueing causes jitter and high end-to-end latency, while loss causes visible gaps. These are intrinsic QoS measures; the player’s responsiveness/quality judgement is QoE. Use queue management/priority, adaptive bitrate/FEC or concealment, and reduce avoidable encode/playout buffering, acknowledging the smoothness-versus-latency trade-off. Trap: “more bandwidth” does not necessarily lower queueing delay.

Verified local-paper basis

Verified families: 2017/18 Q1(i–iii), Q3(i), 2023/24 Q4(a), 2024/25 Q4(b) and Q6(a–b) (latency, QoS/QoE, VoIP and jitter buffers).

Topic-specific traps and diagnosis

  • Equating bandwidth with low latency.
  • Proposing an unlimited buffer for interactive media.
  • Ignoring loss and encoder/decoder delay.

Exam marking checklist

  • Did I identify the user-facing symptom?
  • Did I distinguish latency from jitter?
  • Did I state the cost of my control?

Paper-years note

VoIP/RTP and multimedia appear in older papers, while latency, QoS and web performance become more prominent in 2023/24-2024/25. Map each lecture's terminology before relying on an older format.
